note.explanation: Metals generally lose electrons and form positive ions called cations. How easily a metal loses electrons is related to its reactivity: metals that lose electrons easily are more reactive. Alkali metals such as sodium and potassium are highly electropositive and react vigorously. Magnesium and calcium lose their outer electrons less easily, so they are less electropositive than alkali metals. Aluminum is also highly electropositive and reacts readily with mineral acids.
examples: Sodium and potassium react vigorously with water and halogens.
Aluminum reacts readily with mineral acids to form salts and hydrogen.
note.checkAnswer: Alkali metals are more electropositive than alkaline earth metals.
note.simple: Electropositive metals give away electrons. The more easily a metal gives away electrons, the more reactive it is.

note.title: Electropositive Character of Metals
steps: A metal loses one or more electrons.
Losing electrons forms a positive ion, called a cation.
A metal that loses electrons easily is more reactive.

note.answer: Alkali metals are more electropositive than alkaline earth metals.

explain.title: Meaning of electropositive character
explain.body: Metals generally have a tendency to lose electrons to form positive ions called cations. This property is called the electropositive character of metals.

explain.title: Electropositive character and reactivity
explain.body: This property is also related to the reactivity of the metals. Metals which lose electron or electrons easily are considered more reactive.

explain.title: Alkali metals and alkaline earth metals
explain.body: Alkali metals (Na, K) are highly electropositive and react vigorously with water and halogens. Alkaline earth metals (Mg, Ca) lose their outer electrons less easily and thus they are less electropositive than alkali metals; their reactions towards water and halogens are also less vigorous.

explain.title: Aluminum
explain.body: Aluminum is also highly electropositive metal. It reacts readily with mineral acids to form salts and hydrogen.

mistakes: Do not say that electropositive metals gain electrons; they lose electrons and form positive cations.
Do not reverse the comparison: alkali metals are more electropositive than alkaline earth metals.
Do not say Mg and Ca react more vigorously than Na and K with water and halogens; the section says their reactions are less vigorous.
When answering the short question, give both parts: metals lose electrons easily and non-metals gain electrons easily.
